claims.text: The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are initially solid.
The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase homogeneous solid solutions.
Atomic-size mismatch in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles generates local strain fields.
Chemical short-range order or local compositional heterogeneity in these nanoparticles generates local strain fields.
Local strain lowers the energy barrier for melting at particular regions of a nanoparticle.
Strain-rich regions nucleate melt at lower temperatures than other regions of the same particle.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles consequently undergo spatially heterogeneous premelting and melting.
Their localized melting begins at lower global temperatures than melting in compositionally simpler nanoparticles.
Distinct melting fronts will emerge from strain-rich regions in the HEA nanoparticles.
Single-metal or bimetallic baseline nanoparticles with less size disparity and less chemical ordering will melt more uniformly.
The baseline nanoparticles will exhibit fewer localized melt-nucleation sites than the HEA nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles smaller than approximately 20 nm under controlled premelting and melting conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to bulk material.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under extremely rapid nonequilibrium heating or cooling.
Particle-size distribution, exact composition, and heating rate may affect the magnitude and spatial heterogeneity of melting.
Prior in situ TEM and HEA-strain studies support the proposed strain-mediated melting mechanism.
A lack of statistically significant earlier localized melting in the HEA particles relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
